segments.say: Elena's déjà vu wasn't about one object. It wasn't the mug, or the rug, or the coat hooks taken alone. It was the whole arrangement: a narrow hallway, a staircase on the right, a landing with a window. What if that overall arrangement, the layout, is what triggers the feeling? That's the idea we'll follow in this chapter, and it comes with some of the most inventive experiments in the field.

Our minds are very good at remembering the layout of places. We remember that the kitchen is at the back, that the bathroom is up the stairs, that the corner shop is two streets from the station. Much of this knowledge is stored in the hippocampus and nearby areas, which hold something like a mental map. And maps, as we know, can look alike even when the places they describe are different.

The idea that the hippocampus holds a map has a clear origin. In 1971, John O'Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky recorded from single cells in the hippocampus of rats, and found cells that fired only when the animal was in one particular place. O'Keefe later shared a Nobel Prize in 2014 for the discovery of what are now called place cells, and the work changed how we think about memory for space.

show.what: The hippocampus as a spatial map

segments.say: Why does this matter for déjà vu? Because the same structures that handle space also help to judge whether something is familiar. If a new place has a layout that is very similar to one you've known, the brain's spatial machinery might respond as if it were the old place, and send up a feeling of familiarity, without being able to say which place it matches.

This idea has a name in the research literature. Alan Brown, in his 2003 review, called it the Gestalt familiarity hypothesis. A Gestalt means a whole, a pattern more than the sum of its parts. The suggestion is that déjà vu occurs when a new scene shares its overall configuration with a scene stored in memory, but the earlier scene itself can't be recalled.

Think of two kitchens. One is in a house you lived in at the age of seven. The other is in a flat you walk into for the first time today. The colours, the cupboards and the objects are all different. But the table sits in the same position relative to the door, the window is at the same distance, and the passage to the next room curves in the same way. Your mind may register that match, and miss the differences.

The psychologist most associated with testing this idea is Anne Cleary, at Colorado State University. In a 2008 paper, she set out the case that déjà vu could be a form of familiarity without recollection, set off by similarity to something in memory that the person can't retrieve. And she designed a series of experiments to try to produce the feeling in the laboratory.

show.what: Recognition memory, familiarity, and déjà vu experiences

segments.say: Her earlier work offered the first clue. In 2000, Cleary and Anthony Greene found that people can sometimes tell whether they have seen a word before even when they can't identify it, for example when it is shown as a badly degraded fragment. They called it recognition without identification. The feeling of knowing can be right, even when the mind has no access to what it knows.

In 2009, Cleary, Anthony Ryals and Jason Nomi tested the layout idea directly. People viewed a series of scenes made in a video game, such as a room or a garden. Later they viewed new scenes, some of which had the same spatial layout as a scene they'd studied, but with different objects in it. They were asked whether the new scenes felt familiar, and whether they had a sense of déjà vu.

show.what: Can déjà vu result from similarity to a prior experience?

segments.say: The finding was that scenes with the same layout as a studied scene produced more feelings of déjà vu, but only when the person couldn't recall the earlier scene. If they could say, oh, this is the same as the one I saw before, the eerie feeling disappeared, because the familiarity now had a source. The déjà vu appeared in the gap between a layout match and a failed memory.

Two rooms with the same shape. In the experiments, the new scene and the old scene looked different at first glance, with different furniture, colours and objects. Only the bones of the arrangement matched. That is what real life is full of: places that rhyme with other places, for reasons of architecture and habit, and a mind that picks up the rhyme without being able to say what it rhymes with.

show.cap: Two similar rooms side by side

segments.say: Three years later, the team moved the work into virtual reality. People walked through virtual scenes, and later through new ones that had the same layout of objects in three dimensions, but different objects. Once again, the similar layouts increased the sense of familiarity, and more so for those who couldn't recall what the earlier scene had been.

show.what: Familiarity from the configuration of objects in 3-dimensional space and its relation to déjà vu: a virtual reality investigation

segments.say: Why use virtual reality? Because it lets researchers control the layout exactly, and make it match or differ in a precise way, something you can't do with real rooms. It also lets people move through the scene rather than merely look at it, which is closer to how déjà vu happens in real life, when you walk into a place and the sense of the known arrives as you move.

It's important to say that this is not a closed case. Some of the results in these studies are modest, and other researchers have found that layout similarity doesn't always increase déjà vu. Cleary herself describes the Gestalt idea as one mechanism that might contribute, and not as the only cause. The feeling may well have several routes, and different people, and different episodes, may take different ones.

Let's gather what these studies suggest. Familiarity can be set off by a match in layout. The match can occur without any recollection of the source. The feeling vanishes if the source is found. And this may be just one of several routes to the experience, not the only one.

show.title: What the layout studies suggest
items: Familiarity can be set off by a match in layout
The match can occur without recalling the source
The feeling vanishes if the source is found
It may be one of several routes

segments.say: For Elena, the story might go like this. Years ago, she spent a summer in her grandmother's house, which had a narrow hall and a stair with a landing window. She hasn't thought of that house for a long time, and she couldn't describe its hall today. But the layout is stored somewhere, and the new hallway matches it. The result is a feeling that she knows this place, with no memory to back it up.

show.sub: A hallway with a familiar bone structure

segments.say: We should be honest that this is only a story about Elena, and an imagined one. A neat account of a single case can feel convincing and still be wrong. What gives the layout idea its weight is that it has been tested, in experiments with many people, using scenes whose layouts were controlled. A story is a starting point. An experiment is what makes it science.

So where do we stand? We've seen that the mind remembers layouts, that the hippocampus holds a map, and that Anne Cleary's experiments show that a new scene with an old layout can create déjà vu, especially when the earlier scene can't be recalled. We've also seen that the evidence is real but not complete.

show.sub: What we set out to learn

segments.say: In the next chapter, we'll turn to one of the most intriguing parts of the experience: the sense that you know what's about to happen. We'll look at a recent experiment that put that claim to a direct test.

show.sub: The feeling that you know what's next
